name: Integration & Messaging Patterns

beginner.content:
What is the Message Broker Pattern?

A Message Broker is an intermediary component that sits between producers (senders) and consumers (receivers) of messages. Instead of services calling each other directly, they send messages to the broker, which is responsible for routing, storing, and delivering those messages to the right destination.

Why Use a Broker Instead of Direct Calls?

• Decoupling - the producer doesn't need to know who the consumer is, where it runs, or whether it's even online right now.
• Buffering - if the consumer is slow or temporarily down, messages just wait in the broker instead of the producer's call failing.
• Fan-out - one message can be routed to multiple consumers without the producer doing anything extra.

Real-World Brokers

• RabbitMQ - a traditional message broker implementing AMQP, strong routing capabilities.
• Apache Kafka - a distributed event-streaming platform, often used as a high-throughput broker/log.
• ActiveMQ - a JMS-compliant broker, common in Java EE / Spring environments.

A Simple Mental Model

Producer ---> [ Message Broker ] ---> Consumer A
                     |
                     +--------------> Consumer B
The producer publishes a message once; the broker takes care of getting it to one or many consumers, depending on how the destination (queue or topic) is configured.

expert.content:
Broker vs Brokerless (Direct) Messaging

Not all messaging needs a broker - some systems use "brokerless" messaging (e.g. ZeroMQ) where the endpoints talk more directly. A broker adds an extra hop and potential bottleneck/single-point-of-failure, but in exchange gives you durability, routing logic, monitoring, and easier scaling of consumers. Most enterprise Java systems use a broker because the operational benefits outweigh the added latency.

Common Broker Responsibilities

• Routing - deciding which queue/topic a message goes to, sometimes based on message headers/content.
• Persistence - optionally writing messages to disk so they survive a broker restart.
• Acknowledgement tracking - knowing whether a consumer successfully processed a message before removing it.
• Dead-lettering - moving repeatedly-failing messages aside (see the dedicated Dead Letter Channel pattern).

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What problem does a message broker solve?It decouples producers and consumers so they don't need to know about each other or be online at the same time
Name two popular message brokers used with JavaRabbitMQ and Apache Kafka (also ActiveMQ, a JMS-compliant broker)
What is the tradeoff of adding a broker?Extra network hop / latency and an additional piece of infrastructure to run and monitor, in exchange for decoupling, buffering, and easier scaling

beginner.content:
What is the Message Queue Pattern?

A Message Queue is a store-and-forward channel that holds messages in (roughly) the order they arrive, until a consumer is ready to process them. It models a one-to-one logical relationship: even if several consumer instances are listening, each individual message is delivered to and processed by exactly one of them.

Why It's Useful

• The producer never blocks waiting for the consumer to be ready.
• Bursts of traffic get smoothed out - the queue simply grows temporarily instead of overwhelming the consumer.
• If the consumer crashes mid-processing, an unacknowledged message can be redelivered.

JMS Queue Example (Illustrative)

A JMS Queue destination is the classic Java example of this pattern - each message put on the queue is picked up by only one consumer, even if multiple consumers are listening:

expert.content:
Queue vs Topic

AspectQueueTopic
Delivery modelPoint-to-point - one consumer gets each messagePublish/Subscribe - every subscriber gets a copy
Multiple consumersCompete for messages (load balancing)Each receives every message independently
Typical useWork distribution (task processing)Event broadcasting/notifications

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
If 3 consumers listen on the same queue, how many of them process a given message?Exactly one - queues implement point-to-point delivery, not broadcast
What happens to a message if no consumer is currently listening?It waits in the queue (store-and-forward) until a consumer becomes available, assuming the queue is durable/persistent

beginner.content:
What is Publish/Subscribe?

In Publish/Subscribe (Pub/Sub), a publisher sends a message to a named channel (a "topic"), and every subscriber currently listening on that topic receives its own copy of the message. This is the direct opposite of a queue's one-consumer-per-message behavior.

Where It's Used

• Broadcasting an event (e.g. "OrderShipped") to multiple independent interested services (billing, notifications, analytics) without the publisher knowing or caring who's listening.
• Kafka topics and JMS Topic destinations are both real implementations of this pattern.
JMS Topic Example (Illustrative)

expert.content:
Durable vs Non-Durable Subscriptions

A key nuance: if a subscriber is offline when a message is published, does it miss the message forever, or get it when it reconnects?

• Non-durable subscription - the subscriber only receives messages published while it's actively connected; anything published while it's offline is lost to that subscriber.
• Durable subscription - the broker remembers the subscriber's identity and retains messages for it even while disconnected, delivering them once it reconnects.
Kafka's consumer-group offset tracking achieves a similar durability effect by persisting "how far" each consumer group has read.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
How many subscribers receive a published message?All subscribers currently subscribed to that topic each get their own independent copy
What's the risk of a non-durable subscription?Messages published while the subscriber is disconnected are lost to it - it only sees messages published while actively connected

beginner.content:
What is Point-to-Point Messaging?

Point-to-Point describes a channel where, even with many producers and many consumers attached, each individual message is consumed by exactly one recipient. It's the formal name for the delivery semantics that a Message Queue provides - the two terms are closely related, and "point-to-point channel" is often used interchangeably with "queue".

Why Call It Out Separately From "Queue"?

"Queue" refers to the physical/logical destination object; "Point-to-Point" refers to the delivery guarantee that destination provides. The distinction matters because some systems (like Kafka) don't have a literal "Queue" object, but you can still achieve point-to-point-style delivery using a single-partition topic with one consumer in a consumer group.

expert.content:
Achieving Point-to-Point Semantics Without a Literal Queue

Kafka is fundamentally a publish/subscribe log, but you can get point-to-point-style "only one consumer processes this message" behavior by putting all consumer instances into the same consumer group - Kafka guarantees each partition is read by only one consumer within a group, effectively load-balancing messages across the group members the way a queue would.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Is "Point-to-Point" a different technology than a Queue?No - it's the name for the one-consumer-per-message delivery semantic that queues implement; the terms are usually used interchangeably
How can Kafka, which has no literal Queue object, still achieve point-to-point delivery?By putting all consumer instances in the same consumer group - Kafka ensures only one consumer in a group reads a given partition's messages

beginner.content:
What is Request/Reply?

Request/Reply (also called Request-Response messaging) is how you get a synchronous-feeling response over an inherently asynchronous messaging channel. The requester sends a message on a "request" channel and also tells the responder where to send the answer; the responder processes the request and publishes a reply message back to that address.

The Two Pieces That Make It Work

• ReplyTo address - the requester includes the destination it wants the reply sent to (often a temporary, per-request queue).
• Correlation ID - a unique ID attached to the request, echoed back in the reply, so the requester can match a reply to the original request even if multiple requests are in flight at once.
Illustrative JMS-Style Example

expert.content:
Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What two pieces of information make Request/Reply messaging work?A ReplyTo address (where to send the answer) and a Correlation ID (to match the reply back to the original request)
Why is a correlation ID needed if there's already a dedicated reply queue?Multiple requests can be in flight on the same reply channel at once, so the ID is needed to tell which reply answers which request

beginner.content:
What is the Competing Consumers Pattern?

Competing Consumers means running multiple instances of the same consumer, all listening on the same queue, so they collectively "compete" for the incoming messages and process them in parallel. It's the standard way to scale message processing throughput horizontally.

Why It Works Well

• Each message goes to only one consumer (point-to-point), so there is no broadcast fan-out. That is NOT the same as no duplicate PROCESSING: under the at-least-once delivery real brokers provide, a consumer crash or ack timeout redelivers an already-processed message, so consumers must still be idempotent.
• Adding more consumer instances directly increases how fast the backlog drains - no code changes needed, just scale out.
• If one consumer instance crashes mid-message, that message can be redelivered to a surviving instance.

Mental Model

                +----> Consumer Instance 1
                |
Queue  ---------+----> Consumer Instance 2
                |
                +----> Consumer Instance 3
Each message goes to exactly ONE of the three instances - they compete for work, they don't all process every message.

expert.content:
Ordering Trade-off

Competing Consumers trades strict message ordering for throughput: if message A and message B are picked up by two different consumer instances at the same time, there's no guarantee B is fully processed after A, even though A was enqueued first. Systems that need both scaling AND strict per-key ordering (like Kafka) solve this by partitioning - messages for the same key always go to the same partition, which is read by only one consumer, preserving order within that key while still parallelizing across keys.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What's the simplest way to increase message-processing throughput with Competing Consumers?Run more instances of the consumer - they automatically share the incoming workload since each message still goes to only one instance
What ordering guarantee is lost with Competing Consumers?Global message order isn't guaranteed across instances - two messages can be processed out of enqueue order by different consumers running in parallel

beginner.content:
What is a Dead Letter Channel?

A Dead Letter Channel (DLC), or dead letter queue (DLQ), is a separate destination that a broker routes a message to after it has repeatedly failed to be processed successfully (or expired, or was rejected). Instead of retrying forever or silently dropping the message, it gets "parked" somewhere a human or a separate process can inspect it.

Why You Need One

• Without a DLQ, a "poison message" (one that always causes the consumer to throw) can get redelivered endlessly, wasting resources and possibly blocking the rest of the queue.
• With a DLQ, that message is moved aside after N failed attempts, and the rest of the queue keeps flowing normally.
• It gives you a place to inspect, debug, and potentially replay the failed message later.
Illustrative Configuration Idea

expert.content:
Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What problem does a Dead Letter Channel solve?It prevents a repeatedly-failing "poison message" from being redelivered forever or silently lost, by parking it in a separate queue for inspection after a set number of failed attempts
What typically triggers a message being dead-lettered?Exceeding a configured max redelivery/retry count, message expiry (TTL), or explicit consumer rejection

beginner.content:
What is the Message Router Pattern?

A Message Router is a component that sits between a sender and its possible receivers and decides, based on the message's content or metadata (headers), which channel(s) the message should be sent to next. The sender doesn't know or care which receiver will actually process the message.

Why Use a Router?

• Without a router, every producer would need to know every consumer's address and the rules for who handles what - tightly coupling them.
• A router centralizes that routing logic in one place, so producers just send to the router and consumers just listen on their own channel.
• New consumer types can be added by updating the router's rules, without touching the producer at all.

expert.content:
Content-Based vs Header-Based Routing

• Content-Based Router - inspects the message body/payload to decide the destination (e.g. an order's country field).
• Header-Based Router - a Content-Based Router variant that inspects metadata/headers instead of parsing the payload, which is cheaper and keeps routing logic decoupled from the message schema.
• In real systems (Apache Camel, Spring Integration, Kafka Streams branching), routers are typically declared as rules/predicates rather than hand-written if/else chains, so routing logic can be updated without redeploying producers or consumers.

Static vs Dynamic Routing

• Static routing - the set of possible destinations is fixed and known upfront.
• Dynamic routing - destinations can be looked up at runtime (e.g. from a routing table in a database), letting the system adapt without a redeploy.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What problem does a Message Router solve?It decouples producers from consumers by centralizing the decision of which destination a message should go to
Content-based vs header-based routing?Content-based inspects the payload; header-based inspects metadata, which is cheaper and doesn't require parsing the message body
Give a real framework that implements this pattern.Apache Camel's choice()/when() DSL, Spring Integration routers, and Kafka Streams' branch()

beginner.content:
What is the Message Filter Pattern?

A Message Filter sits on a channel and discards (or diverts) messages that don't match a given criteria, so that whatever is downstream only ever sees messages it actually cares about.

Filter vs Router

• A Router sends every message somewhere (it chooses a destination for all messages).
• A Filter may send a message nowhere at all - it simply drops non-matching messages instead of routing them.

expert.content:
Where Filters Fit in a Pipeline

Filters are commonly chained right after a Splitter or a Router, so a large or noisy stream of messages can be trimmed down to just the events a given consumer actually needs to act on (e.g. an alerting service that only wants ERROR/CRITICAL log events, not every log line).

Filtering can happen at different layers: a message-broker-level selector (e.g. JMS message selectors using SQL-like syntax on headers) avoids even delivering non-matching messages to the consumer at all, which is more efficient than filtering after delivery.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
How does a Filter differ from a Router?A Router always forwards a message somewhere; a Filter can drop a message entirely if it doesn't match the criteria
Where is it more efficient to filter - at the broker or after delivery?At the broker (e.g. JMS message selectors), since non-matching messages are never even delivered to the consumer

beginner.content:
What is the Message Translator Pattern?

A Message Translator converts a message from the format/schema one system produces into the format another system expects, so two systems with different data contracts can still communicate without either one adapting to the other directly.

Common Translation Needs

• Different field names/casing between systems (customer_id vs customerId).
• Different serialization formats (XML vs JSON vs Avro).
• Different units or value representations (cents vs dollars, ISO date strings vs epoch millis).

expert.content:
Translator as an Anti-Corruption Layer

In a microservices/legacy-integration context, a Message Translator often doubles as an anti-corruption layer - it insulates a new/clean domain model from a legacy system's messy or outdated data shapes, so the legacy schema's quirks never leak into the new system's code. This is a common companion technique alongside the Strangler Fig migration pattern.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why not just make both systems agree on one schema?Systems are often owned by different teams/vendors or built at different times - a translator lets them evolve independently while still communicating
What's an anti-corruption layer?A translation boundary that prevents a legacy or external system's data model from leaking into and "corrupting" a clean new domain model

beginner.content:
What is the Content Enricher Pattern?

A Content Enricher adds missing data to a message before it's passed downstream - typically by looking the extra data up from another service, database, or cache - because the original message doesn't carry everything the eventual consumer needs.

Typical Example

An "OrderPlaced" event might only contain a customerId. If the downstream consumer needs the customer's full name and email to send a confirmation, a Content Enricher fetches those details and adds them to the message before forwarding it.

expert.content:
Trade-off: Enrich at the Producer vs a Dedicated Enricher

Enrichment could happen at the source (the producer includes everything upfront), but that couples the producer to every possible downstream consumer's needs and bloats every message even for consumers who don't need the extra data. A dedicated Content Enricher step keeps the original message lean and adds data only on the specific path(s) that need it - at the cost of an extra lookup call and its latency/failure modes.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why not have the producer just include all the data upfront?That couples the producer to every consumer's data needs and bloats messages for consumers who don't need the extra fields
What's the main cost of using a Content Enricher?An extra lookup call per message, adding latency and a new failure mode (what happens if the lookup fails or the data isn't found)

beginner.content:
What is the Splitter Pattern?

A Splitter breaks one composite message containing multiple items into several individual messages, so each item can be routed, processed, or scaled independently.

Typical Example

An incoming "BulkOrder" message containing 5 line items can be split into 5 separate "OrderItem" messages, each processed independently (possibly by different competing consumers in parallel).

expert.content:
Splitter Is Usually Paired with an Aggregator

A Splitter alone loses the "this was one original request" context. In real systems, each split message typically carries a correlation ID (the original order ID here) so an Aggregator downstream can later collect all the resulting responses back into one combined result once all the split items have been processed.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is the Splitter pattern's inverse?The Aggregator pattern - Splitter breaks one message into many, Aggregator combines many back into one
What do you need to preserve when splitting a message?A correlation ID linking each split piece back to the original message, so results can later be reassembled or tracked

beginner.content:
What is the (Message) Aggregator Pattern?

An Aggregator collects a series of related individual messages and combines them into one composite message once some completion condition is met (e.g. all expected pieces have arrived, or a timeout elapses). It is the direct inverse of the Splitter pattern.

Completion Strategies

• Count-based - complete once N messages with the same correlation ID have arrived.
• Timeout-based - complete after a fixed time window, using whatever arrived so far.
• Predicate-based - complete once a custom condition on the collected messages is satisfied.

expert.content:
Risk: Partial or Never-Complete Aggregations

If one expected piece of a correlated group never arrives (a message lost, a downstream failure), a purely count-based Aggregator will wait forever. Production implementations almost always combine a completion count/predicate WITH a timeout, so a partial (or empty) result is eventually emitted rather than holding state indefinitely - this trade-off between correctness and liveness is central to designing a real Aggregator.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Name the 3 common completion strategies for an Aggregator.Count-based (N messages arrived), timeout-based (time window elapsed), and predicate-based (a custom condition is met)
What happens if a correlated message is lost and only a count-based strategy is used?The aggregation waits forever - production systems pair a count/predicate strategy with a timeout to guarantee eventual completion

beginner.content:
What is the Idempotent Consumer Pattern?

An Idempotent Consumer is a message consumer designed so that processing the same message more than once produces the same end result as processing it exactly once - with no duplicated side effects (like charging a customer twice).

Why This Matters

Most message brokers offer at-least-once delivery, meaning a message can be redelivered after a crash, network blip, or consumer restart even though it was already successfully processed once. An idempotent consumer makes redelivery harmless instead of dangerous.

expert.content:
Where to Track Processed IDs

The set of "already processed" message IDs must itself be durable and consistent WITH the side effect it's guarding - if the ID is recorded in a different transaction/store than the actual business update, a crash between the two steps can still let a duplicate slip through. The reliable approach is recording the processed-ID check and the business state change in the same database transaction (or using a natural idempotency key already present in the data, like a unique order ID, instead of a separate tracking table). This ties directly into the Outbox pattern used on the producing side of the same problem.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why would a message ever be delivered twice?Most brokers guarantee at-least-once delivery - redelivery can happen after a crash, timeout, or consumer restart even if the message was already processed
What's the risk of tracking processed-message IDs in a separate store from the business data?A crash between updating the two stores can leave them inconsistent, letting a duplicate slip through - they should be updated in the same transaction
Give a real-world idempotency key example.A unique order ID or a client-generated request ID (idempotency key) sent with a payment request, so retries of the same request are recognized as duplicates

cheatNotes: Message Broker - intermediary that routes/delivers messages, decoupling producers from consumers
Message Queue - point-to-point: each message goes to exactly one consumer
Publish/Subscribe - broadcast: every subscriber gets its own copy of the message
Point-to-Point - the delivery semantic (one consumer per message) that queues implement
Request/Reply - async request-response using a ReplyTo address + Correlation ID
Competing Consumers - multiple consumer instances on one queue to scale throughput in parallel
Dead Letter Channel - parks repeatedly-failing messages aside instead of retrying forever or dropping them
